goal.title: The goal
paragraphs: Grow your net worth: the holding’s cash and shares, plus what your companies own, less what they and the holding owe. There is no end; play as long as you like.
You start with a holding and some money: start your first business from the dashboard. Run it well, open or buy more, and keep clear of unpaid bills.

time.title: Time
paragraphs: The clock at the bottom runs a day at a time, at the speed you pick, or a week at once. What you change applies at the start of the next day, and waits in the list above the clock until then.
The clock stops for news you choose (menu, When to pause), and the game saves itself every month and when you leave.

holding.title: Your holding
paragraphs: The dashboard shows your net worth, what needs doing, each store at a glance, your profit week by week, and the news.

Each company has its finances: the holding puts cash into it, takes a dividend out of its profit (the state takes 30%), and the company borrows. The bank lends on what your stores earn, and more if the holding guarantees it; open or buy a store without the cash and it offers to lend the rest.

store.title: Your store
paragraphs: Choose what is on the shelves and at what price, against what shoppers in that city think normal. Staff each part of the day: too few and shoppers wait or walk out; none and the store is shut.
Spend a share of sales on marketing to build goodwill, hire a manager to run things for you, or open a second shop: a supermarket, where a site has the room.

Holding lists your companies. Hire a director for any of them there: they hire the managers, close stores that keep losing money, grow it as far as you allow, borrowing if you let them, and write to you each month.
Start a subsidiary from Holding to keep a new business apart: it has its own cash, books, loans and director, and if it fails the rest is safe.

orders.title: Orders
paragraphs: Buy stock from suppliers. Each has its lead time, payment terms, minimum order and discounts. Fresh food spoils, so order what will sell before it does.

reports.title: Reports
paragraphs: See profit and loss week by week or month by month, where shoppers came from and went, and what they wanted and could not find. Buy market studies to learn about a city before you open there.

market.title: The market
paragraphs: Follow the economy: inflation, the central bank's rate and unemployment rise and fall through booms and recessions, and shoppers spend accordingly. Profit is taxed every January.
Companies publish their accounts each year. See every rival, its stores and prices, and the cities with their vacant sites.

deals.title: Buying and selling businesses
paragraphs: Every store has an asking price: its fittings and stock, plus a few years of what it earns beyond a fair return on them. A store losing money sells for well under what it holds, a bargain for whoever can turn it round.

Buy a rival’s store with one of your companies’ cash, borrowing the rest on what both earn, or a whole company with its stores, cash and debts out of the holding’s cash, the company borrowing part of its price on its own earnings. Sell a store to the chain best able to pay. Gains are taxed with the year’s profit; rivals buy struggling stores too.

tips.title: Tips
paragraphs: Keep the shelves stocked: shoppers who find them empty go elsewhere, and some stay there.

Price close to what shoppers expect; dear works where people can afford it. Cutting prices wins shoppers, but most leave when prices rise, and thin margins earn little in a small shop: discounting pays on a supermarket's volume, or for a few months to start a new store.

Watch the cash. A bill unpaid for a month means liquidation, and a recession can empty the till. Each company keeps a cushion for wages, rent, loan payments and January's tax: below it, managers buy only the essentials.

finance.bargainsNone: No rival store is losing money just now. Every store and company has its asking price under World, competitors.
finance.bargainsSome: Rival stores losing money sell for well under what they hold. Every other asking price is under World, competitors.
finance.billsOnWay: Unpaid bills and orders on their way
finance.cushionHint: {length} of wages, a month's rent, loan payments and this year's tax
finance.dividendsFromThis: Dividends can only come out of this
finance.loanTermsGuaranteed: {rate} a year, {left} monthly payments left, guaranteed by the holding
finance.addCapitalBody: Move the holding’s cash into the company. It can only come back as dividends, out of profits. The holding has {cash}.
finance.addCapitalBodyParent: Move {parent}’s cash into the company. It can only come back as dividends, out of profits. {parent} has {cash}.
finance.dividendBody: Pay the holding out of the profit the company has kept, {kept}.{tax}
finance.dividendBodyParent: Pay {parent} out of the profit the company has kept, {kept}.{tax}
finance.dividendTax: The state takes {rate} of it as dividend tax.
finance.repayBody: Pay back early, with the interest due so far. {left} is left.
finance.directorPitch: A CEO runs the company for you: hires the store managers, closes stores that keep losing money, and grows it as far as you allow. They write to you each month.
finance.keepsStores: Keeps the stores as they are
finance.sendsProfit: sends you the profit each month
finance.keepsProfit: keeps the profit in the company
finance.runsFor: Runs {company} for you: hires a manager for any store without one, closes stores that keep losing money, and grows it as far as you allow.
finance.gradeHint: Cuts their managers' misjudgment by {cuts}; misjudges what a new store would earn by up to {error}
finance.howFar: How far they may grow it

growth.none: Keep the stores as they are

growthHints.none: Rivals that grow will take shoppers
growthHints.invest: When the extra space would pay for itself
growthHints.open: Where one would pay back soonest, run by the strategy below
growthHints.buy: Losing stores whose price would pay back

finance.growRateHint: New shops a month, as a share of the chain's shops in each country.
finance.ofItsTrade: {share} of its trade in a country
finance.beyondPaceHint: Faster than that, they pick worse places and every shop of the chain is run worse, the more the further past it.
finance.nationalPaceHint: Each costs about {cost} to fit out and is run from head office, opened where it pays back soonest within the strategy's limit.
finance.nationalAnywhere: No region picked: anywhere in the countries the company trades in.
finance.boughtThisYear: On {amount} of goods bought over the last twelve months
finance.marketingDirector: What pays best, as your CEO judges
finance.whatSizeBuysHint: The more a company buys, the less its goods cost, in every shop it has. Marketing across a country pulls more shoppers the bigger the chain that spends it.
finance.onlyEarnings: Only from what the company earns
finance.onEarningsBuy: On its earnings, never on the holding’s guarantee. They also buy profitable rivals, if those pay back within {years} years
finance.onEarnings: On its earnings, never on the holding’s guarantee
finance.sendMe: Send me what's left each month
finance.sendMeHint: Beyond a reserve and the year's tax, once works and new stores are paid for
finance.moreThanBank: More than the bank lends: up to {amount}
finance.guaranteeOn: If the company fails, you pay what is left. You can still back {amount}.
finance.guaranteeOff: Lent on {years} of your stores' earnings: up to {amount}.
finance.firstPaymentHint: The first payment, falling as it is repaid
finance.bankBoth: {credit} on {years} of your stores’ earnings, less what they owe; {guarantee} more if the holding guarantees it
finance.bankCredit: {years} of your stores' earnings, less what they owe
finance.bankGuarantee: Only if the holding guarantees it: your stores’ earnings carry no more yet
finance.bankNothing: Your stores’ earnings and the holding’s guarantee carry no more
finance.taxSoFar: Tax on this year's profit so far
finance.cushionPitch: Your managers buy stock in full only with free cash beyond the cushion. Below it, they buy a few days of their best sellers, so the company can still pay wages, rent, the bank and January's tax.
finance.cashLessBills: Cash less unpaid bills and orders on their way
finance.dividendsWhere: Taken from the dividends the holding receives, at the rate where it is: {country}
finance.taxBase: On {base} made there this year, after losses carried
finance.taxByCountryHint: Each country taxes what the company's shops made there; costs beyond the shops, such as interest and a CEO, are shared by sales.
finance.taxRatesHint: {reduced} on a year's profit up to {limit}, billed each January
finance.dividendsHint: Taken from the dividends the holding receives
finance.taxHint: Profit kept in the company is taxed once; paid out as dividends, it is taxed again. Investing in stores defers both.

market.countriesHint: Each country has its own ups and downs, mostly in step with the others, and its own prices, wages, suppliers and taxes. One central bank sets the rate for all of them. Inflation on the right.
market.countryTaxesHint: Corporate tax on what a company's shops make here, whoever owns them; dividend tax on what those who live here pay themselves.
market.nationalHint: The whole country by formula, from its national statistics (Eurostat, 2022): what households spend before VAT, and each chain's share of its trade. The chains are fictional, and grow, shrink or fail with their margins.
market.tileKey: Shade: your share of the region · figure: your shops
market.whereRoomHint: What one more shop would add to profit a year, run as your CEO would run it, soonest paid back first. Fitting out costs more where wages and rents are higher.
market.regionsHint: Shops run by formula across the country, region by region: a CEO opens them where they pay back soonest. The more of yours a region holds, the less each new one adds. Where wages and rents are higher, shops are fewer and each sells more.
market.chainsHereHint: Shops each has in the region.
market.offerAgainst: By their earnings they are worth {worth}.
market.noBuyer: No chain can pay that now.

sellBody.one: Your shop goes to them for {price}, paid now. It cannot be undone.
sellBody.other: Your {count} shops go to them for {price}, paid now. It cannot be undone.

market.chainYours: This chain is yours: its shops are among yours across the country.
market.chainHint: Its price is what its fittings are worth, plus its earnings beyond a fair return on them. The bank lends on its earnings as well as yours.

buyChainBody.one: Its shop becomes {company}’s for {price}, run by formula under its name.
buyChainBody.other: Its {count} shops become {company}’s for {price}, run by formula under its name.

market.buyChainLoan: The company borrows the {amount} it lacks, on the earnings, over {term}.
market.yoursAsleep: Your shops here are run by formula, in your company's books. Taking them in hand plays the district in full: you or their managers run them from then on.
market.takeInHandBody: The district wakes for good: its shops and households are played day by day, and your shops there are run like your others. It can't go back to sleep.
market.runByFormula: By formula until someone opens there
market.whereToOpenHint: What a well-run new shop might earn in a settled year, before tax, on the best free site for it. Only rivals in its own trade count. A rough guide: about half of these come within 8,000, and some are far off.
market.plannedHint: Figures for businesses you don't own are estimates.
market.spentHere: Spent here on this trade, a year
market.newShopShare: A new shop's share of it
market.newShopProfit: Its profit before tax, a year
market.openedClosed: Shops opened / closed since the start
market.noSiteFor: No free site here is big enough for this.
market.prospectHint: By estimate, for a well-run shop past its first months, at normal prices. A restaurant takes nothing from a grocer, so only rivals in its own trade count.
market.competitorsSummary: {count} rival companies{local}: accounts, stores, prices and asking prices
market.citiesSummary: {cities}{vacant} vacant sites: markets, stores and sites to open on
market.cutBack: Households cut back and trade down
market.changeSinceStart: Prices, wages and buying power: change since the start.
market.moreOnEconomyPitch: What each figure does, and the economy month by month
market.historyBuilds: The history builds up month by month.
market.okun: Unemployment follows the cycle with a lag (Okun's law); when it runs high, wages grow more slowly and households spend less.
market.filingsKnown: Companies file their accounts every January: last year's sales and profit are public. Prices are what shoppers pay against what they think normal in that city.
market.filingsUnknown: Companies file their accounts every January; until then, only their stores and prices are known.
market.symbolicHint: It owes more than it is worth: a symbolic euro, debts included
market.companyPriceHint: Its stores at their asking prices, plus its cash, less its bills and loans
market.buyTomorrow: You buy it tomorrow, if you can still pay.
market.paidBorrowShort: Paid from the holding’s cash, and up to {credit} borrowed on its own earnings: the holding needs {short} more.
market.paidShort: Paid from the holding’s cash: it needs {short} more.
market.paidCanBorrow: Paid from the holding’s cash, or partly borrowed on its own earnings. Its stores, cash and debts become yours.
market.paidCash: Paid from the holding’s cash. Its stores, cash and debts become yours.
market.theirLastSales: At their last four weeks' sales and today's costs
market.upToPayLess: Up to {amount}, so you pay less
market.storesEarnMonth: Its stores earn about {amount} a month
market.tomorrowBody: Tomorrow, at the asking price then. Its stores, cash, bills and loans become yours, and its stores are yours to run: stock them yourself or hire managers.
market.storeEarnsMonth: The store earns about {amount} a month
market.needsMoreBorrow: It needs {amount} more: borrow it, or put the holding’s cash in from Finance first.
market.keepsStock: It keeps its stock, staff, prices and shoppers, and the deal goes through tomorrow at the asking price then. From then on, reorder for it or hire a manager.
market.economyHint: Supplier prices, rents and what shoppers expect to pay follow prices; staff and managers follow wages. When wages outpace prices, households buy more premium and care less about price; the better-off always do. Loans cost the central bank rate plus the bank's margin.
market.levelsHint: Against the usual: what shoppers here expect to pay, what staff and managers earn, and how well off households are. Suppliers charge their own country's prices.
market.marketHintFirst: A year, at today's prices · the next census comes in January
market.marketHint: A year, at today's prices · {change} since last year
market.subsidiaryHint: A subsidiary is a separate company in your holding, with its own cash, books, loans and CEO: if it fails, the rest is safe. Pick a city and a neighbourhood, then a vacant site for its first store. To buy a going company instead, see World.
market.businessHint: Pick a country, a city and a neighbourhood, then a vacant site: you choose its name and the capital it starts with when you open. To buy a going business instead, see Finance.
market.vacantDetails: {area} m², room for {most} · location {location} · rent {rent} a month · fitting out from {cost}, {days} days
market.newCompanyNote: A new company has no earnings yet: the bank wants the holding’s guarantee
market.fittingCosts: Fitting out costs {cost} and takes {days} days. Budget for stock, staff and rent too.
market.vacantEnlarged: {area} m², enlarged to {opening} m² for it · location {location} · rent {rent} a month · fitting out and works from {cost}, {days} days
market.opensEnlarged: It opens enlarged to {opening} m² from the site’s {area} m²: the works are in the cost, and the rent is for {opening} m².
market.ownBooks: Its own books: if it fails, the rest is safe
market.cycleDeep: Its downturns run deeper than most.
market.cycleMild: Its downturns run milder, and often on their own.
market.cycleUsual: Its ups and downs are the usual ones.
market.cityHint: Its shoppers spend {market} a year. Prices {prices}, incomes {incomes} and wages {wages} of the usual.

rails.title: Rails
rails.worth: What is on the rails is worth {worth} of new, on average. Shoppers pay less for clothes that have sat.
rails.eachLineHint: How old each line is, what it is worth and its markdown
rails.clear: Clear the old to a jobber
rails.clearBody: A jobber takes the {units} pieces over six months old for about {paid}, a share of the {cost} they cost. The loss is written off.
rails.nothingOnOrder: Nothing on order for this shop.
rails.managerOrders: Your manager orders collections ahead, marks down what fades and clears what is spent.
rails.youOrder: You order yourself. Collections come weeks ahead and cost less in bulk; quick deliveries cost more. Order more than sells while new, and it fades on the rails.
rails.gone: This shop is no longer yours.
rails.linesHint: Clothes keep their appeal for a month or two, then lose it month by month. Price them down as they fade, or they stop selling.

software.title: Software
software.startPitch: A small team, one product, the world's customers. Hire well and raise money to get there.
software.name: Name
software.countryHint: Its people are paid at that country's wages, and it pays tax there.
software.capitalHint: The holding has {cash}. People cost {low} to {high} a month each; investors buy shares in rounds once you have a team.
software.capitalHintParent: {company} has {cash}. People cost {low} to {high} a month each; investors buy shares in rounds once you have a team.
software.ownCompanyHint: Its own company, under the holding: a rival may buy it whole, and investors buy into it alone.
software.besideHint: Beside {company}’s other businesses: a round sells a share of all of {company}, and a rival buys the software alone, paying {company}.
software.howProduct: Your product starts {gap} points under the market's standard, which rises a point a month. It sells once within {launch} points of it.
software.howPeople: Your people build it. The best counts in full and each next one less, so a few of the best beat many ordinary people.
software.howMoney: Customers pay every month. Investors pay for a team that builds faster than the market, and later for growth.
software.chartHint: Your product's lead over the market's standard month by month, against the best rival's.
software.chartEmpty: The race fills in month by month.
software.aheadLine: {lead} points against the standard; best rival {rival}
software.buildingLine: {gap} points from a first version that sells

launchIn.one: First version in about a month.

software.launchNever: At this pace, never: the market moves faster than your team builds. Hire people who build faster.
software.productHint: Ahead of the standard, it draws far more of the customers who change products each month, and keeps more of its own. The further ahead, the more work each point takes.
software.noTeam: Nobody yet: hire people to build the product.
software.designerDoes: builds at half pace and adds appeal
software.marketHint: Each asks what their track record is worth. Their true level shows after {months} months at work: a record can flatter or undersell. One of the best is worth about ten ordinary people.
software.full: The team is full. Let someone go before hiring.
software.priceHint: The market's average is {reference}. Dearer draws fewer and loses more.
software.marketingHint: Marketing draws customers from the first version on. Each euro more brings fewer; a product ahead also spreads by word of mouth.
software.fromMarketing: At this budget, marketing wins about {count} new customers a month.
software.breakEven: Pays its way at about {customers} customers.
software.standardRises: The standard rises a point a month as everyone builds.
software.marketHint2: Shares are of every customer in the world.
software.worthRevenue: A year of revenue, {revenue}, times {multiple}, with its cash, less what it owes.
software.worthTeam: Before it sells much, investors pay for the team: {team}, with its cash, less what it owes.
software.offerYours: Your share: {yours}. The offer stands until {date}.
software.acceptBody: You get {yours} for your share, taxed as a gain. Its people and customers go to {rival}.
software.acceptBodyAlone: {company} gets {price}, a gain taxed with its profit, and trades on without it. Its people and customers go to {rival}.
software.raiseHint: Investors buy up to {max} of the company at what it is worth, one round every {months} months.
software.nextRound: The next round can come from {date}.
software.cannotRaise: Investors see nothing to buy yet: hire a team that builds faster than the market.
software.raiseBody: They put {money} into the company, worth {worth} before the round. You keep {stake}.
software.shutDownBody: Its people leave and its customers go elsewhere. The company keeps its cash.
software.gone: This software company no longer runs.

sales.rivalsHint: Rivals bid only while they have room. They improve their goods after losing to you, and cut their prices; a chain’s own plant makes its goods first and sells the rest.
sales.contractGone: This contract is no longer running.
sales.pendingTomorrow: Your change is put to the chain tomorrow.
sales.requestBody: {chain} asks for {price} a unit: about what rivals would bid now. Turn it down and it puts the rest out to tender. Answer by {date}.
sales.refuseBody: The contract ends and {chain} puts the rest out to tender, where you may bid again.
sales.askHint: The chain pays what still beats what rivals would bid; ask too much and it says the most it would pay.
sales.breakHint: Breaking it also costs reliability, which chains weigh in your later bids.
sales.breakBody: You pay {fee} and {chain} puts the rest out to tender.
sales.title: Sales desk
sales.marketHint: What shops in the countries it serves spend on the goods it makes: every chain and the independents.
sales.reliabilityHint: A contract month short of what was promised costs a penalty and reliability; chains weigh reliability against your price.
sales.noContracts: No contract yet: bid on chains’ tenders.
sales.noTenders: No chain is seeking a supplier for its goods just now.
sales.independentsOff: You don’t sell to independent shops: set a discount under “Sells to” on the factory’s page.
sales.independentsOn: At {discount} off what wholesalers charge, less what reaching scattered shops costs. Your share grows slowly toward what your price and quality earn.
sales.gone: This tender is no longer open.
sales.tenderAsks: {units} a month for {months} months in {country}, of goods at least {floor} points against the standard. Bids close {date}.
sales.producerPriceHint: What chains pay producers buying direct: bids are weighed against it.
sales.belowFloor: Below what the chain asks: develop the line in the lab first.
sales.recent: Lately such tenders went for {low} to {high} under the producer price.
sales.fitsNoHint: Beyond what it makes at three shifts: each month short costs a penalty and reliability. Enlarge it first, or bid on smaller tenders.

lab.title: The lab
lab.chartHint: Each step up is a generation; the market catches up in between.
lab.chartEmpty: The chart fills in month by month once the lab takes up a line.
lab.idle: The lab is idle. Pick a line and a budget to start its next generation.
lab.budgetHint: Up to {amount} a month, spent only while a line is on the bench.
lab.noTeam: No key people yet: the budget alone does the work.
lab.engineerDoes: speeds the work and saves material

reputed.one: as reputed, shows in a month

lab.letGoConfirm: {person} leaves for good and won't come back on the market.
lab.marketHint: Each asks what their track record is worth. Their true level shows after {months} months at work: a record can flatter or undersell.
lab.noCandidates: Nobody is on the market this month.
lab.full: The lab is full. Let someone go before hiring.

factory.sizeHint: A plant or an industrial site makes far more than your shops sell: it sells the rest to chains through tenders, and to independent shops, from its sales desk.
factory.enlarging: Being enlarged to the next size, {size}: done {date}.
factory.enlargeBody: It costs {cost} and takes about {months} months, while it keeps running at its size. {capital} of it comes from the holding’s cash.
factory.gone: This factory is no longer yours.
factory.earnsHint: Against buying, at its last four weeks
factory.wouldHavePaid: Your shops would have paid the wholesalers
factory.atMarket: Sold to your shops at what their wholesalers charge them.
factory.boughtIn: Beyond its capacity, your shops bought {units} from their wholesalers.
factory.paysFrom: It pays from {use} of its capacity.
factory.stoppedHint: Stopped: your shops buy from their wholesalers, and the site is still paid.
factory.shiftCost: Each shift makes {units} a day and costs {amount} a day, used or not.
factory.notMadeYet: not made yet: what the wholesalers charge
factory.linesHint: What your shops pay for each, and what it costs to make: materials and a share of staff, site and freight.
factory.abroadHint: Abroad takes {days} more days and pays freight of {freight} of the price.
factory.localHint: Its goods don't travel: it delivers only in its own country.
factory.rivalsHint: Rivals' shops buy from it when it's their cheapest supplier, from what your shops leave: more use of it, and cheaper goods for them.
factory.canSpare: It can spare {units} more this month.
factory.closeConfirm: Close {factory} for good? Your shops will buy its goods from their wholesalers again, and building it again costs as much.
factory.makes: It makes {products}: your shops then buy them only from it.
factory.noShops: None of your shops sells these goods yet.

unitsMonth.one: A month, at your shop's last four weeks
unitsMonth.other: A month, at your {count} shops' last four weeks

factory.planHint: Its capacity used, what your shops would still buy from wholesalers, and what it would earn a month against buying.
factory.name: Factory name
factory.buildNote: Its staff are paid at that country's wages, and its profit is taxed there.

refusals.notForBids: That company can’t be bid for.
refusals.premiumRange: The premium must be above nothing and at most 100%.
refusals.chainNeedsCompany: A chain’s shops need a company: bid with one of yours.
refusals.bidTooLow: A bid of {amount} a share is already open: offer more.
refusals.payoutRange: The dividend must be from 0 to 100% of profit.
refusals.debtRange: Aim for at most six years of profit in debt.
refusals.notARival: Only a smaller listed rival of its sector and country.
refusals.bidAlreadyOpen: A bid is already open for it.
refusals.noRaiderBuyer: No raider can pay for it all.
refusals.subsidiaryListed: A subsidiary is listed with its parent, not on its own.
refusals.listedShareRange: Sell from 5% to all of it; new shares, less than all.
refusals.earnsTooLittle: It must earn, or for software sell, before it lists.
refusals.noSector: The exchanges have no sector for its business.
refusals.onlyThePlayerTrades: Only you trade on the exchanges.
refusals.moreThanItsShares: That’s more shares than it has.
refusals.noRequest: The chain has asked for nothing.
refusals.priceRefused: The chain would pay at most {amount}.
refusals.tenderNotServed: That factory doesn’t deliver to the tender’s country.
refusals.factoryLargest: It is already the largest size.
refusals.belowQualityFloor: Its goods are below the quality the chain asks.
refusals.bidRange: A bid must be more than nothing and at most {amount}.
refusals.noSoftware: This game has no software market.
refusals.softwareClosed: That software company no longer runs.
refusals.softwareOnly: Its CEO needs a goal for each business.
refusals.hasSoftware: It has software already: one to a company.
refusals.listedRestructure: A listed company’s shareholders own what it holds: it stays as it is.
refusals.outsideInvestors: Its investors own part of what it holds: it stays as it is.
refusals.notEnoughCashIn: the company taking it needs {amount} in cash
refusals.notEnoughCashForTax: not enough cash to pay the dividend tax on the way up
refusals.underItsOwn: A company can’t sit under one of its own.
refusals.mergeWhere: A company merges into its parent, or into one beside it.
refusals.hasSubsidiaries: Move or sell its subsidiaries first.
refusals.sellPartsFirst: Sell its plants, software and shops across countries first: buyers of a company take shops alone.
refusals.softwarePriceRange: The price must be more than nothing and at most {amount}.
refusals.softwareMarketingRange: Marketing must be from nothing to {amount} a month.
refusals.roundShareRange: A round sells at most {count}% of the company.
refusals.roundTooSoon: Rounds come at most every {count} months.
refusals.nothingToRaise: Investors see nothing to buy yet.
refusals.madeInHouse: {product} comes from your factory: order it there
refusals.notYourFactory: the actor does not own this factory
refusals.noFactories: there are no factories to build
refusals.shiftsRange: a factory runs from 0 to {count} shifts
refusals.cannotPayFactory: the company cannot pay the building cost of {amount}
refusals.noNational: this game has no national figures to open shops in
refusals.formatNotNational: {format} cannot be run by formula across the country
refusals.nationalCountRange: open from 1 to {count} shops at a time
refusals.cannotPayNational: the company cannot pay the fitting out of {amount}
refusals.regionCeiling: the competition authority lets no owner hold more than {count}% of a trade’s shops in a region
refusals.nationalCeiling: the competition authority lets no owner hold more than {count}% of a trade’s shops in a country
refusals.noChainBuyer: no chain can pay for these shops
refusals.unknownOffer: that offer is no longer open
refusals.offerWithdrawn: the chain can no longer pay what it offered
refusals.nationalRateRange: a CEO grows a chain by 0 to {count}% a month
refusals.servesEachCountry: say for each of the {count} countries whether it delivers there
refusals.servesItsCountry: a factory always delivers in its own country
refusals.factoryLocal: this factory's goods don't travel to other countries
refusals.rivalDiscountRange: a discount for rivals must be from 0 to 50%
refusals.factoryNotMaking: the factory isn't making anything yet
refusals.factoryDoesNotServe: the factory doesn't deliver in this store's country
refusals.factoryExclusive: the factory sells only to its owner's shops
refusals.factoryFull: the factory can't spare that much this month
refusals.labBudgetRange: a lab's budget is between 0 and {amount} a month
refusals.keyPersonTaken: they are no longer on the market
refusals.labFull: a lab holds at most {count} key people
refusals.notYourKeyPerson: they don't work for the actor
refusals.notFashion: these goods don't go out of fashion
refusals.clearanceAge: the age to clear from can't be negative
refusals.factoryMinimum: {product}: the factory takes at least {count} units per line
refusals.noDirectors: there are no CEOs for hire
refusals.notYourStore: the actor does not own this store
refusals.notYourCompany: the actor does not own this company
refusals.notEnoughHoldingCash: not enough cash in the holding
refusals.notEnoughParentCash: not enough cash in the company that holds it
refusals.notEnoughCompanyCash: the company does not have that much cash
refusals.dividendsFromProfits: dividends can only come out of retained profits
refusals.cannotBackGuarantee: the holding’s cash cannot back that guarantee
refusals.bankWantsGuarantee: the bank wants the holding’s guarantee
refusals.bankCannotLend: the bank cannot lend that much
refusals.moreThanLoan: that is more than is left on the loan
refusals.bankWillNotLend: the bank will not lend that much
refusals.managerNeedsDuty: give the manager at least one duty
refusals.notListed: the store does not list this product
refusals.alreadyListed: the store already lists this product
refusals.marketingCap: at most a quarter of sales can go to marketing
refusals.nothingForSale: businesses never change hands in this scenario
refusals.alreadyOwnStore: the actor already owns this store
refusals.justChangedHands: the store has just changed hands
refusals.brandedStoreName: a branded shop takes its brand's name
refusals.wakeToOpen: opening there brings the district into play instead
refusals.noBuyer: no one can afford the asking price
refusals.alreadyOwnCompany: the actor already owns this company
refusals.borrowOverPrice: the company cannot borrow more than its price
refusals.noLoanOnEarnings: the bank will not lend on its earnings
refusals.noStartingStore: the scenario has no store to start with
refusals.nameRule: a name must be 1 to {count} characters, without spaces at either end
refusals.cushionRange: a cushion holds 0 to {count} days of wages
refusals.bankLendsAtMost: the bank lends at most {amount} on the company's earnings
refusals.termRange: the term must be from 1 to {count} months
refusals.floorNotOffered: the site can’t open a shop of {count} m²
refusals.cannotPayOpening: the company cannot pay the opening cost of {amount}
refusals.staffEachSlot: give staff for each of the {count} slots
refusals.staffRange: staff per slot must be from 0 to {count}
refusals.belowMinimum: {product}: {supplier} sells at least {count} units per line
refusals.overCapacity: {product}: more units than the store can hold
refusals.cannotPayPrice: the company cannot pay the asking price of {amount}
refusals.holdingCashShort: not enough cash in the holding for the asking price of {amount}
refusals.bankLendsItAtMost: the bank lends it at most {amount} on its earnings
refusals.fitOutTooDear: fitting out costs {amount}, more than you have

stocks.raidersHint: Raiders buy what their style finds cheap, and a raider bids for companies it holds enough of; they may bid for yours once you hold half or less.
stocks.overReference: {premium} over what it was worth to its holders
stocks.tendering: Your shares are offered into this bid.
stocks.notTendering: Your shares stay out of this bid.
stocks.holdingBorrowHint: The bank lends the holding against the shares it buys, on their profit and what it can guarantee; if an instalment can’t be paid, it sells them.
stocks.companyBorrowHint: The bank lends the company on its earnings and the target’s, then on the holding’s guarantee.
stocks.notEnoughForBid: Its cash and what it borrows must cover {cost}, every share it lacks.
stocks.rivalHint: The company you control pays with debt.
stocks.freeFloatAccepts: about {share} of the free float would accept
stocks.bidHint: Open 30 days; it needs over half. Over 90%, the rest are bought out and it leaves the exchange.
stocks.chainBidHint: Open 30 days; it needs over half. A chain won joins the bidding company as its shops, the rest bought out.
stocks.noLongerYours: You no longer control this company.
stocks.growthHint: Fast: a point off the margin, three more of sales a year. Slow: half a point on, one less.
stocks.debtHint: Borrowing up to it is paid out a quarter of the way at a time.
stocks.noRivals: No smaller listed rival in its sector and country.
stocks.sellItHint: The richest raider that can pay bids for it all at a premium, and your shares are offered into its bid.
stocks.listItPitch: Sell part of it to the market
stocks.keepControl: Over half: no one can take it over. Its dividends are shared with its shareholders.
stocks.openToBids: Half or less: raiders and rival chains may bid for it, and the other shareholders decide.
stocks.newSharesHint: New shares bring their money into the company.
stocks.yourSharesHint: Selling the holding’s own shares brings the money to it, taxed as a gain.
stocks.notEnough: That’s more than the holding has.
stocks.closed: The exchanges open on the first day of the game.
stocks.noHoldings: The holding has no shares yet. It buys them with its own cash, not your companies’.
stocks.howPricesMove: A price is what a company earns, times what the market will pay for it today. The market’s mood runs ahead of the economy: euphoric late in a boom, panicked in a crash.

chartSince.one: Its price on the first of each month, over {count} month.
chartSince.other: Its price on the first of each month, over {count} months.

stocks.delisted: It no longer trades on its exchange.
stocks.sectorMedianHint: Sector medians are taken across the sector’s listed companies in every country.
stocks.noFullYear: No full financial year published yet.

booksBasis.formula: Fixed assets at the sector’s capital intensity (Eurostat net fixed assets over output, 2022), revalued at current prices, less net debt.
booksBasis.chain: Shop fittings at cost less depreciation, and cash. The chain reports no borrowings.
booksBasis.software: Fixed assets estimated at the sector’s capital intensity. No borrowings are reported.
booksBasis.producer: Fixed assets estimated at the sector’s capital intensity. No borrowings are reported.

stocks.judgedHint: Analysts go by their own idea of its worth: often right, but swept along by the market’s mood and late to see a turn. Management is rated on its record.
stocks.indexHint: Buying the index buys a little of each company, as much as it is worth on the exchange, none counting for more than 15%, and pays you their dividends.
stocks.impact: An order this big moves the price by about {change}.
stocks.buyHint: Your order goes through at the next day’s price.
stocks.sellHint: Your order goes through at the next day’s price. A gain is taxed where you live, once past losses on shares are set against it.
stocks.taxHint: Dividends are taxed when paid, gains when you sell.

screener.title: Screener
screener.entry: Filter and sort the {count} listed companies

cheap.title: Cheap against their past
cheap.hint: Price to earnings under 20 and a fifth under its usual, run at least averagely

income.title: Paying over 5%
income.hint: with debt under three years of profit

growing.title: Sales growing 10% a year
growing.hint: the last four quarters against the four before

fallen.title: Fallen 30% in a year, still well run

strongBuys.title: Analysts’ strong buys
strongBuys.hint: where analysts see the most above the price first

screener.yourOwnHint: pick the figures and the limits

sorts.belowUsual: by price to earnings against its usual
sorts.upside: by what analysts see above the price

screener.none: No listed company meets all of these. Loosen a criterion.
screener.tableHint: Tap a column to sort by it, again to reverse. Sales: the last four quarters against the four before. Debt in years of profit.

past.star: {count} years at the head of {employer}’s shops

pastNowhere.seasoned: {count} years running shops across a region
pastNowhere.star: {count} years at the head of a chain

does.payback: takes shops that pay back in up to {months} months, against your strategy’s {usual}
does.thickCushion: keeps a thicker cushion of cash
does.thinCushion: keeps a thinner cushion of cash
does.credit: borrows at most {share} of what the bank would lend
does.fastPace: left to judge, grows faster than their grade runs well
does.slowPace: left to judge, grows slower than they could
does.asItIs: applies the brief as it is

lost: A loss, but within what the plan allowed for.

lost: I’m holding back on new shops until this passes.

earned: Every euro saved shows in the results.
lost: I’ll find the costs to cut.

directors.shortlistHint: A new shortlist comes on the first of each month. Character changes how they apply your brief; grade, how well they judge.
